title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Irrigation servicing
audience: Owners of small Australian irrigation servicing businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on skill, experience with controllers and valves, any registration the work needs, the range of work offered and the cost of running the business. A technician who can check, reschedule and report on a system in one visit can justify a higher rate than one who only checks zones. No independent irrigation servicing hourly rate was found. The nearest sourced reference is the Melbourne landscaper rate of $50, $72 and $99 per hour (What's the Damage, verified 1 November 2026). That is a landscaping rate, not an irrigation technician's rate, so use it only as a loose reference. Do not cut your rate to win work.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Travel between sites, quoting, reports, admin, training, tool upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid hours in a year, subtract the non-billable time, and divide the costs by the billable hours that remain. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours, a general range rather than an Australian figure (Jobber, 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). Check your own log against that range. If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the rate must be about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week (100 divided by 60).

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, any registration fees, vehicle, test equipment, software, phone, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. On-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026). Confirm with a registered tax agent how leave and superannuation apply. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate, then review it about every three months (Business Victoria, undated).

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: A short check or a single-zone fix can cost more in time than it earns, because travel and the trip to the site do not shrink with the job. Set a minimum that covers travel, set-up and admin, and state it before the visit. The method is to take the full cost of the visit and divide it by one minus the target margin (Contractor+, 23 September 2026; figures illustrative, method only). For example, a full visit cost of $40 (illustrative) at a 30 per cent target margin gives a minimum of $57.14. No sourced rule on minimum or call-out charges for Victoria or NSW was found, so check before publishing a price sheet.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, any registration fees, vehicle, test equipment, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: an irrigation technician's log shows that only 60 of every 100 paid hours can be billed, but the technician plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate, and what should the rate be built from?
workedExamples.reasoning: The rate would come out about 40 per cent below the level the costs require, because the costs must come out of 60 billable hours, not 100 (60 divided by 100 is 0.6). The rate is built from billable hours, the registration and insurance costs are added as overheads, the minimum for a short check is set, and the result is checked against the local evidence before publication.

equipmentAndPpe: Annual costs and income worksheet with registration and insurance lines
Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a servicing rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from the owner's own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Setting a servicing rate from installation prices.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep installation figures out of the servicing rate, and build it from your own costs and billable hours.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. Misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). The sources read for this variant do not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm how leave and superannuation apply to the owner's own pay with a registered tax agent before the rate is published.

This lesson does not grant any registration or licence. Confirm which registration applies to the regulated work before pricing it. In Victoria, the VBA lists non-agricultural irrigation as a registered plumbing class. NSW irrigation licensing is not confirmed.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short irrigation visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly cost.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range, not an Australian figure. Supports: billable time typically 60 to 80 per cent of working hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Figures labelled illustrative; no country stated. Only the method is used.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

What's the Damage, 'Landscaping cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/landscaping-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026. Cost guide; not a regulator. Supports: landscaper $50 / $72 / $99 per hour, used only as a loose reference.
